en: Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
In this Troṭala Tantra, however, she is remembered by the name Tvaritā;
she is declared to be the bestower of success, this vidyā which can assume any form at will.
Spoken by the God of gods, this supreme knowledge was disgorged from the mouth of Suparṇa; it is the most secret of secrets, even among the secret ones.
And it is the supreme knowledge among secret things; that knowledge fulfills all desires and has already been extracted from the Tantra of ten hundred thousand verses.
From this [tantra], thousands of other tantras have emerged;
from this, moreover, the nine-syllable mantra known as Tvaritā should be understood.
She is the crusher of all serpents, the agitator of the seven netherworlds;
she is the source of all seeds and is proclaimed as the very womb itself.
This supreme knowledge is secret, remembered as the mistress of both the secret and the non-secret;
it is the sovereign of all secrets, for it is the most excellent means for swiftly accomplishing what is otherwise difficult to achieve.
She is the heart of all goddesses, the sovereign of the lords of the Siddhas and Siddheśvarīs;
she is the Vidyā who accomplishes all rites and the mistress of the entire universe.
Bestowing success in all desires both in this world and the next,
she is difficult to attain even for all the gods, the ṛṣis, and the yogins.
In age after age, by this method, the gods, gandharvas, kinnaras,
sages who have seen the power of austerity, and the holders of the knowledge of the munis, have attained perfection.
The Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas, as well as Siddhayogeśvarī,
are the heart of all the gods, Siddhas, and Yoginīs.
O Mistress of the lords of ten lakhs, this vidyā crushes all the nāgas dwelling in the seven netherworlds throughout the three worlds.
For the benefit of human beings, this much fruit has been brought down;
this knowledge was previously perfected even without the practice of ascetic observances.
Human beings in the mortal world apply themselves to all actions, both auspicious and inauspicious;
by means of this [knowledge], they indeed achieve success quickly and attain liberation, both supreme and non-supreme.
Desiring the state of a Vidyādhara, a universal monarch, or a lord of the gods,
they perform serpent-sports in the mortal world, filled with curiosity.
Those who desire the state of moving through the sky together with the lords of the Siddhas and Yogas,
and who desire death at their own will, [should proceed] as far as Sadāśiva.
They bestow the accomplishment of sovereignty, while the accomplishment of wealth is manifold;
through that [accomplishment], one certainly performs rites such as summoning and so forth.
Killing, expulsion, subjugation, paralyzing,
cutting, splitting, the breaking of enemy armies, and the destruction of mechanical devices.
She is the deluder of all the wicked, including the rākṣasas who feed on fear;
whoever should maintain this vidyā, even by reciting it but once—
Indeed, that man is seen blazing like the many-feathered Garuda facing the wielder of the trident,
once he has recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times during the morning twilight.
Whoever should remember this is not afflicted by diseases;
first there is the perfection of speech, followed by the triad of attraction and severance.
Arise! [I shall explain] the doctrine of otherness, the fourth, the practice of poison;
the fifth, the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva); and the sixth, the state that bestows nirvāṇa.
This Vidyā, the mistress of all lords of action, was created as a cow of plenty;
O Tārkṣya, I shall now utter this Vidyā along with its defining characteristics.
I shall fully explain the characteristics of those who perform no ritual action and are devoid of vows and sacrifices; listen to this in brief.
Aiṃ, conjoined with two hūṃs, adorned with the two words khecarī,
followed by the letter beyond the classes (kṣa), the visarga, and indeed strīṃ, hūṃ, kṣaiṃ, and phaṭ— this is what is remembered.
This knowledge is a great knowledge; it is Tārkṣya herself, the sovereign of the gods.
Since there is no ritual action without this, I shall now declare its application.
In this *Uttarottara*, one learns the application [of mantras] through their forward and reverse order, and by means of their combined and individual conjunctions.
Without application, how can there be accomplishment? How can there be wise action?
For many millions of mantras have arisen within this scripture.
The mantras established in various scriptures and their applications therein are difficult to find;
I shall explain their practical applications in brief, and not in detail.

HŪṂ SVE CA CHE KṢAḤ. By this [mantra], one may even raise up someone bitten at the time of application. If [the mantra] is devoid of the visarga, it does not cause [the victim] to fall [into unconsciousness]. If joined with the bindu, the person becomes free from poison.
Having consecrated the left hand eight thousand times with the mantra,
one should write the name on the ground and sprinkle it nine times;
by whose name this is done, that person is seized by fever at that very moment.
One should strike the name together with a *visarga* upon black mustard seeds; having smeared that [mixture] on the hand, one may travel a hundred *yojanas*.
Then, if one desires to bring about well-being, one should write the name in milk upon birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) for the sake of all vidyās.

One should cast [the mantra] recited once into milk; or else, by drinking it, the person becomes healthy. *Hūṃ chakṣaḥ*. This practice is difficult even for the thirty gods to obtain. In whatever place this moves, it causes the seven netherworlds (*sapta-pātāla*) and the lords of serpents (*bhujaṅgeśvara*) to flee. This practice [destroys] the sin of being bitten by a snake in three [days].
One should contemplate [the mantra] in the various locations: by [contemplating it] on the head, the heart, and the two feet, one becomes free from poison at that very moment.

Having encountered even a hundred palas of poison, one removes it; through the power of the mantra, one desires it and causes it to transfer elsewhere. By this very practice, joined with the syllable *hūṃ* at the beginning and end, one paralyzes pestilence.

It paralyzes with a malevolent mind hosts of *nāgas*, *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *sākinīs*, *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, as well as elephants, horses, *śarabhas*, tigers, lions, leopards, and so forth; it causes trees to wither, or it paralyzes carts and mechanical devices. It renders those with the faces of *nāgas* free from poison through the entire *vidyā* by means of the mind.

By reciting this very practice once at its conclusion, releasing the syllable *hūṃ*, there is summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), elevating (*utkarṣaṇa*), and paralyzing (*stambhana*); through paralyzing, cutting, and further cutting— whatever is required for restoration— this very practice is unfailing, and accomplishment proceeds through speech.
It causes the seizing of children by spirits to fall away and destroys the grasp of those who seize hair.
*Phaṭ strī kṣe hūṃ*.
Having understood this application, why would human beings suffer?
Such a practice as this will not be found in any other tantras.
Having gone to a solitary, uninhabited place, pure and having bathed, facing eastward,
and being intent on performing the protection ritual, the practitioner should diligently recite the *lakṣa* [of mantras] with a steady mind if he desires the highest accomplishment.
But then, at the fourth hundred thousand [recitations], a vision is seen at night.
Making a great and terrible roar and a loud, boisterous laugh,
the Great Secrets arrive, O Mistress of the Lords of Siddha-yoga.
The practitioner, however, must offer well-prepared *argha* and *pādya*;
at the end, by means of the mantra and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, the Guhyakas are satisfied.
O son of Vraja, O great hero, the state of moving through the sky is very difficult to attain;
therefore arise, O great hero, for you are an adept with this very body.
Surrounded by his powers (śaktis), he shall wander through the divine worlds;
and at the end of the great dissolution, having become Śiva, he shall move through the sky.
This successful application, however, is never born anywhere;
for even when successful, it is deficient in its parts, and you should remember the injunction of Manu.
He brought about the destruction of his enemies and mastered all branches of knowledge;
at the beginning and end of the ritual application, the wise one should employ the six-syllable mantra.
One should swiftly cause the Cakravartin king to be slain by means of [the mantra] devoid of the syllable *phaṭ*, joined with *hūṃ* at the beginning and the end.
When one bitten by the serpent Kāla arrives, he shall send him to Satīrtha; having taken four grains of sugar, Śarkaroṭa shall cast them into the Nāga-pool.
One should employ the syllable *hūṃ* at the beginning and the syllable *phaṭ* at the end;
by this very application, it is consecrated seven times with seven [repetitions].
First, one should agitate the mighty Nāga king Karṇa;
in the second stage, the powerful lord of the Nāga kings moves from his place.
In the third [vision], the parasol of the three worlds together with its surroundings is seen;
in the fourth, the deity Vāsuki, the king of the nāgas, is seen.
If this serpent, arrogant with poison, is seen by you even with effort,
he will reduce Jambudvīpa to a heap of ashes in a mere moment.
The wise one should withdraw the ritual application itself from the deity;
having performed the *vaṣaṭ* at the beginning and the end, the king, being satisfied, shall depart.
This practice has been fully explained as bestowing accomplishment and being exactly desired;
now I shall also declare the application for every mantra.
That by which all the gods, siddhas, ṛṣis, and kinnaras have known—
how accomplishment is achieved without affliction in Jambūdvīpa— that I shall now declare.
They are accomplished through the Mānavīya [tantra], even when devoid of vows and sacrifices:
HŪṂ KHECA CHEKṢA STRĪṂ HŪṂ KṢE PHAṬ.
O Queen of the Gods, O Lord of Śaṅkha, this knowledge was formerly held by me, Tārkṣya, and was kept most secret; now, through its expansion, it is accompanied by instruction.
O Goddess, when uttered even once, it brings about the destruction of all sins;
[it surpasses] thousands of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) and hundreds of yogic meditations (yogadhyānas).
Recited but once, this vidyā is not defiled by dharmas or adharma;
it goes indeed to the supreme station where the god Maheśvara dwells.
I shall now declare its ritual procedure by which men attain success;
having first performed the purification of the body, one should thereafter commence the rite.
When this vidyā is recited even once, purification of the body certainly occurs;
through speech, he attains perfection, and indeed, there shall be no one equal to him.
Having bound the excellent mudrā, one should recite the gentle mantra;
the one bitten by the serpent will rise up immediately—what need is there to speak further?
By means of the syllable *phaṭ*, that *praṇītā* (consecrated water) is indeed empowered; when recited with the *visarga* [the letter *ḥ*], it causes [the spirits] to fall.

Having uttered the mantra together with the *visarga*, one should sprinkle the *praṇītā*; then the *ḍākinīs*, *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, and whatever other species there may be, as long as they do not release the *praṇītā*, they are burned and dissolved.
One should release the *praṇītā* vessel with a gentle disposition and recite the mantra;
then they will certainly attain gentleness.
By chanting a hundred thousand syllables, one shall become the lord of treasures.
By doubling [the practice], one becomes a king endowed with virtues and sovereignty.
The goddess Yakṣiṇī, who can assume any form at will, perceives through the three qualities (guṇas);
impelled by the cosmic age (kalpa), O Great Hero, he sports with her.
Through these four qualities, the Great Siddhi attains the state of the Yogīśvarī;
becoming equal to her as a Khecarī, one sports according to one's desire.
Through five qualities one may wander as Brahmā, just like Brahmā himself;
through six qualities, however, the state of Viṣṇu is attained—of this there is no doubt.
Wherever Viṣṇu resides, success for that person shall certainly be firm;
there the Great-Being sports, and the abode of Lakṣmī is present.
Equal to Hari and possessed of great heroism, the Lord of the World may wander;
having recited the vidyā seven times, they go to the god Sadāśiva.
Freed from merit and demerit, the lord of practitioners may wander as a great hero; he shall become equal to Mahādeva. Having recited the vidyā eightfold, he shall go to the state of nirvāṇa.
Out of affection for you, I have declared this purifier of the path to liberation;
having understood and practiced this, one is not born again as a mortal.
She indeed goes to the supreme abode, reaching which one does not return;
O Ekavīra, this great vidyā is remembered as swift in her singular power.
For the benefit of human beings, this has been told by me to Tārkṣya;
therefore, men afflicted by laziness do not perform their duties.
If one endowed with devotion should recite [this mantra] at the three times of day according to one's desire for qualities and sovereignty, I shall grant him wealth.
Even for such a person, the Yakṣa Dhanada shall bestow abundant wealth at the command of the Goddess;
provided that, having performed worship, even a single individual should remember [the deity] once a day.
In his house there was always established a cow that granted all desires;
he who would worship [the deity] every day at one time with all kinds of grain.
By means of invocation, the nine and seven [fires] are present in the house through manifest prosperity;
by the daily oblation of sesame seeds, one attains a hundredfold increase and a state of threefold division.
For him, that supreme goddess of knowledge shall become directly manifest as the granter of desires;
she bestows manifold enjoyments and whatever else is desired by the mind.
He who, having become fully empowered (sakalībhūta), meditates according to his desire while being prosecuted,
is not slain by anyone— not even by the messengers of death or the great planetary spirits.
Indeed, by whom can he be slain, even by those corrupted by great diseases?
O Supreme Goddess, I shall now describe the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa for this Vidyā.
I shall now fully proclaim the division of the syllables, the arrangement for the worship of the deities,
the fire-puja, and the mandala of the Goddess.
Having first performed the ritual placement (karanyāsa), one should apply [the mantras] to those limbs:
the syllable *hūṃ* on the left thumb and the syllable *khe* on the index fingers.
One should place the letter *ca* in the middle finger, the letter *ucche* in the ring finger, and the letter *kṣa* in the little finger; thus one should perform the placement in the left hand.
Furthermore, on the right side, I shall describe again in due order as before:
the syllable *strīṃ* is on the little finger, and the syllable *hūṃ* is on the ring finger.
One should place the syllable *kṣe* on the middle finger and assign the syllable *pha* to the index finger;
the syllable *ṭa* is placed on the right thumb—this is proclaimed as the purification of the hands.
O Tārkṣya, hereafter I shall explain to you the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa):
one should place the syllable *hūṃ* on the head and the syllable *khe* upon the circle of the face.
One should place the letter *ca* at the region of the throat and the letter *tcha* at the heart;
the letter *kṣa*, together with the *visarga*, is situated in the middle of the navel.
One should place the syllable *strīṃ* at the secret place, the two syllables *hūṃ* on the thighs,
the syllable *kṣe* on the two knees, and the syllable *phaṭ* on the two feet.
From this arrangement of the syllables *akṣara*, the body of the Vidyā becomes manifest in an instant;
indeed, it is seen blazing by gods and asuras, both divine and non-divine.
I shall describe the visualization of the deities of the syllables, O Great Goddess:
the syllable *hūṃ* is the entire deity, the Lord of Time, the Sovereign of the World.
The syllable *kha* has Vāyu as its deity and is situated in space;
the syllable *ca* has Indra as its deity and is the Lord of the Lords of Siddhas and Yogas.
The letter *ccha* is the supreme power (*paramāśakti*) that cuts through the ten knots;
it is known by the name *kṣurikā*, leading to supreme liberation.
The severer of all bonds, she who, when remembered, is not afflicted by delusions;
she who transcends the categories through emission, the Great Mistress of the Lord of Tārkṣya.
He is Mahābhairava; Ananteśa is Khageśvara, the feminine form, and the deity of the three—this is the supreme heart of the yogis.
The syllable *hūṃ* has Rudra as its deity; it is Sadāśiva, free from all ailment.
The syllable *kṣe* is the supreme source (*paramāyoni*), the secret origin that bestows spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The letter *pha* is herself the goddess Umā, the mistress of the three worlds;
she is the source of all yoginīs and the sovereign of all masters of yoga.
The letter *ṭa* is the supreme deity, the Lord of the Lord of Half-Measures;
it has the form of a half-moon, is subtle, the supreme ether, both transcendent and immanent.
O Tārkṣya, the conceptualization of the deities has been explained according to their divisions;
now I shall fully describe their worship, by which one certainly attains success.
Having first performed the ritual placement of syllables (*akṣaravinyāsa*) and the rite of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) within oneself,
one binds the earth with the Visarga-syllable that transcends the classes of consonants.
The invocation, the seat, the water offering (argha), the bathing, and likewise the dismissal—
all this must be performed by the practitioner with the *visarga* [mantra].
Having placed the syllable *hūṃ* on the pericarp, one should place the syllable *khe* on the eastern petal,
the syllable *ca* in the southeastern position, and the syllable *cche* on the southern [petal].
One should place the syllable *kṣa* with the visarga in the southwestern direction,
the syllable *strīṃ* in the western direction, and the syllable *hūṃ* on the northwest petal.
The practitioner, devoted to meditation, should place the syllable *kṣe* in the north;
he should place the syllable *phaṭ*, the supreme power (*paramāśakti*), in the northeastern direction.
The syllable *kṣa* together with the *visarga*, [should be placed] in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
this indeed is the prescribed rule for worship and for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*).
Even a practitioner devoid of fortune attains success in no time at all;
for this Vidyā is of great power, created in ancient times, and not composed of syllables.
She is the bestower of wealth and the giver of liberation, and she is the destroyer of poison and pride.
HŪṂ CCHEKHE CA. This application causes even one bitten by a snake to speak and raises them up.
By means of that which is joined with the syllable *phaṭ* at the beginning and end, one causes [the victim] to fall.

HŪṂ STRĪṂ HŪṂ. This practice is supremely effective. By means of this narrative recitation, one causes [the subject] to rise; it destroys even hundreds of poisons; and one transfers [the power] wherever one desires. By this very practice, when empowered eight thousand times—
One should cover the corpse bitten by [a snake] with a cloth.
One should contemplate this practice in three places; then, upon rising, one becomes free from poison.

By this very application, having seen or not seen a woman, one should bind the Praṇītā mudrā and recite [the mantra] up to one thousand times; then one attracts her even from a hundred yojanas away. By adding the syllable *ca* and joining it with *hūṃ* at the beginning and end, one dispatches her.
Khe kṣaḥ.
With the mind focused on the ritual application (*prayoga*), one establishes as if dead—mangled, fallen, or shattered—all those merely seen in disputes.

One even dispatches one bitten by a venomous snake to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). By means of [the mantra] joined with the *phaṭ* syllable at the beginning and end, the wombs of *brahmarākṣasa*s, as well as *bhūta*s, *preta*s, *piśāca*s, quartan fevers (*cāturthaka*), and so forth, are cut away simply through recollection.
One performs the rite according to one's own will. *Haḥ phaṭ hūṃ phaṭ cche phaṭ*. This is the ritual application:

by offering a thousand oblations of human ashes while uttering the name of anyone, even a sovereign universal monarch (*cakravartin*) will be killed within half a watch (*prahara*). One should take a hundred crow feathers and offer them as oblations with the juice of a mad-dog.
It banishes even a lord of wealth and master of riches from his country; it does not allow him to remain in the city as before.
By this very practice, one becomes free from poison by using bath-water for snakes and insects.

Having performed a swift worship with sesame flowers, one becomes free from the poison of eight thousand snake-stings. As many as three times the number of oblations offered into the fire, so many thousands of snakes will arrive upon the earth.

They stand at the gateway of the covering; with them he plays, performs actions according to his own will, and draws forth the queens of the lords of serpents from the seven netherworlds (pātālas). They become his followers behind him; what need is there to mention his fear of being bitten? He performs rites through the application of killing: *HŪṂ KHEPHAṬ CHEDANAṂ*. [This applies to] the beginning and the end.
HŪṂ STAMBHANAM | KHESTRĪKHE | This practice should be recited three hundred thousand times;

one becomes accomplished in the power of moving through the sky and attaining the state of a Vidyādhara, becoming equal to a Lord of Yoga (Yogeśvara). [It effects] the summoning, raising up, killing, driving away, sweating, and piercing of great kings and lords of serpents.

It also removes poison and pride. For one bitten by a deadly snake, having consecrated either an umbrella-stick or a pair of sandals seven times with this mantra, one sends them to the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*). *Kṣaḥ strīṃ kṣaḥ*. This application is as follows:
upon seeing an enemy with a weapon raised in his hand, one should recite [the mantra] three times over the left hand and show the weapon.
He paralyzes [the opponent] at that very moment, and stands like a servant.

He gives whatever one desires. Having mixed yellow pigment (rocana) and lac together, and having recited the mantra three times, one should apply a tilaka on the forehead and in the middle of the topknot; then, while performing this practice and reciting the mantra mentally, one should look upon the king—even if he is angry, he will become pleased with one's wealth.
O King, perfumes, flowers, fruits, a sword, clothing, or sandals—having consecrated these with three recitations, they should be given; what need is there to mention women or lowly persons?
But he who would give even a single [mantra] could bring Purandara himself under his control;
so too for one who recollects the application [of this mantra] at the time of sexual union with women.
She desires only this man for her recitation and no other;
likewise, she desires perfumes, flowers, ointments, betel, and yellow pigment.
By the practice of reciting it once, one indeed becomes the master of women;
by reciting it once and bathing in water, one obtains the fruit of a thousand sacred fords.
He who recites the Sarvavidyā and undergoes the consecration of all mantras shall not be afflicted by diseases, even by those most terrible and severe.
One is not smeared by merit or demerit;
they go to the state that is free from affliction, O Lord of Birds, having become auspicious, and having gone there, one does not return.
O Mistress of the Lords of Half-Seals, I shall now describe the characteristics of the mudrās:
having placed the two hands with the palms facing upward, one should press the middle fingers with the thumbs.
Having raised the two index fingers and made the two arms like a staff, this Mahāmudrā is bound; by that means, it shall lead to the attainment of siddhi.
Or as many times as one recites it with diligence, that [mantra] shall bestow success;
having extracted the essence of this Tantra consisting of eleven thousand [verses].
The Tvaritā, which bestows all desires, is proclaimed as belonging to Troṭala;
it is celebrated as having a measure of two hundred verses.
O Lord of Birds, this must not be told to just anyone;
it must be guarded, for through lack of protection, ruin will occur, just as wealth is lost to thieves.
Oṃ! The one named Hiraṇyapuruṣa, who has deep-set eyes and great strength—sent by him, having been released, may he leave this place; svāhā!
[The thirty-fifth chapter of the eleven-thousand-verse *Troṭalottara Mahātantra*]
[Thus ends the *Tvaritājñānakalpa*.]
Now I shall fully explain the form of the Goddess, O Lord of Birds;
listen now with focused attention, for it is beyond doubt and perfectly clear.
Resembling the ocean of milk, a pearl necklace, the kunda flower, the moon, frost, and nectar.
Blazing with the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning, she was extremely difficult for gods and asuras to behold. || 1 ||
She has six faces and eighteen eyes, with parted lips and a beautiful smile;
for every single syllable of the Goddess, there are two arms and two eyes.
They were complete with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament—
nāga-bracelets, armlets, necklaces, anklets, and girdles.
In her right hands, she holds weapons: a sword, a staff, an eye, a discus, a mace, a trident, an arrow, and a divine spear that grants boons.
A bell, a noose, a *haṃsa*, a conch, a lotus, a goad, a bow,
the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), or the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) shine upon the goddess’s left hands.
The divine Dharma-siṃhāsana has the splendor of a Himalayan peak;
[the deity seated upon it] is terrifying, with a lolling tongue, blazing eyes, and sharp fangs.
Tearing asunder the worlds with his sharp-pointed claws like oyster-shells,
he appeared as if about to consume all that is moving and stationary, his upper body raised and his face turned upwards.
Tvaritā is mounted there with her left leg hanging down,
while her right leg is doubled back and placed upon the top of her foot.
With her left foot placed upon a thousand-petaled lotus,
she is clothed in divine garments, and her facial complexion is like that of Brahmā.
The middle [form] is greenish-white, adorned with a crown of *japa* beads;
she has nine heads and a serpent-umbrella, adorned with the jewels upon the hoods. This is declared as the secret in the eleventh thousand [verse] of the *Mata*.
Thus, O Tārkṣya, I have told you this for the sake of the swift arrival of Troṭalā.
If it has been clearly explained, one should reveal this treasury of wealth to another;
it must be guarded with great effort, like the fetus of a mother by her paramour.
[Thus ends the Troṭalottara.]
Oṃ, homage to Tvaritā!

May that goddess Su-pracaṇḍā— the fierce weapon of the Mother-goddesses impelled by the syllable *Hūṃ*, who holds in her right hands a bow, an arrow, a trident, the gesture of granting boons, a discus, a spear, a mace, and a staff that crushes the pride of the enemies of the gods— bestow [blessings] upon us.
They meditate upon that peerless, Śaṅkara-like perfection.
Even as she plays, she holds in her left hands a noose,
a goad, a threatening gesture, a bell, a conch, a lotus, and a formidable, radiant bow;
she who is adorned with a multitude of excellent flowers and shines like a cluster of stars.
May she, whose body hairs stand erect with joy, accomplish our desired purpose. || 2 ||
May she who is called Tvaritā protect you— she whose earrings blaze like two endless *kulikas* resting upon her staff-like arms,
whose throat-plate is clearly adorned with a shimmering necklace,
and whose beautiful hands bear the *cakras*, Takṣaka, and Śaṅkhapāla as bracelets.
The Blessed One, Caṇḍikā, is the three worlds. || 3 ||
She by whom the entire snare-net of Māyā was severed for her servants, who placed the serpent Karkoṭaka— fierce with its fangs— at the site of her waist-knot;
and whose two lotus-feet have the serpents Padma and Mahāpadma as their anklets— may she, the creator of the three worlds, [protect us].
The mother Puṣṇa provides nourishment for men. || 4 ||

Those who meditate upon you in their hearts— you whose face is radiant with laughter and the sound of the syllable *kṣaḥ*, whose eyebrows are arched like a bow, who bestow a lotus as resplendent as the rainbow of Indra, and whose eyes flicker like the moon, the sun, and fire— they become sovereigns of the Vidyādharas.
O Mother, they attain the state of Viram.

She who, though having assumed a female form, is the Blessed Lady worshipped by the three worlds; she whose foot-luster is made radiant by the jewels in the circles of crowns belonging to Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods;
she whose head is marked by the crescent moon and whose three eyes are like lotus petals; she is Kālī, the Terrifying One.
May Gaurī, Samarī, and Mātaṅginī protect you. || 6 ||
Having performed the ritual for obtaining the sacred site according to the rules, one should drive stakes made from milk-tree wood into the earth,
supported by cords, in the ten directions. Then,
being pure and having assumed the mantra-body, whatever the practitioner of Śiva meditates upon, that shall be accomplished without obstacle.
One soon attains that desired object which is otherwise difficult to obtain.
Having uttered the syllable *Hūṃ*, she who possesses a radiant halo of light within her heart, whose breasts bear the likeness of the lofty frontal globes of an elephant and are adorned with pearls,
takes a delightful and pleasing seat upon the pericarp of a white lotus.
With her feet placed upon the back of a threatening lion, she bestows her own multitude of boons.

O Goddess whose weapon is the sound *phaṭ* and who provides perfect protection, for those who meditate upon you, the eight great supernatural powers (*mahāsiddhi*) remain as if in the palm of their hand;
and even the hundreds of faults arising from the contemptuous gaze of spirits, ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, and serpents, as well as the state of nirvāṇa itself, take refuge in them.
And then, by the grace of the Goddess, all the more so. || 9 ||
O Śivā, your seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of three and a half syllables is renowned as difficult for people to obtain; yet those who know it and recite it according to the sequence—
whether separately, combined, or even by its halves, quarters, or eighths— their minds uplifted, have passionate women rushing before them.
The playful waves of the celestial river fall down.
Whatever desire one contemplates while dwelling upon the earth,

that [desire] generally turns toward them as if resting in their hands, O Giver of Boons; therefore, having abandoned everything else which is more difficult to master, people should serve her alone, who is like a manifest wish-fulfilling creeper.
Furthermore, what more can be said of you, my mother, by those such as me? || 11 ||
Those who constantly recite this hymn to you, O Glorious Mother, and those who listen to it with devotion, or even have it written and kept within their homes—
they rejoice without anxiety, and they have no fear born of thieves, fire, or calamities; for they are honored everywhere and are victorious.
He is beloved upon the surface of the earth. || 12 ||
[Thus ends the Tvaritā-stotra, composed in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter, consisting of twelve verses.]
[Thus ends the auspicious and glorious work.]
Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Resembling the color of a coral sprout, possessing a radiance equal to the joyful sun,
the syllable *hūṃ*— the honored color worshipped by the gods— abides in the foundation.
Having the hue of safflower and saffron, yellow in color, and of great luster;
it is the paralyzer of all beings and bestows the power of flight, which is exceedingly difficult to attain. (2)
O Goddess, that form which resembles pure crystal, possesses a luster like that of lightning, resides in Maṇipūra, and bestows peace. (3)
O Goddess, O Beloved, it stands cutting through that which resembles a water-laden cloud and has the appearance of a swarm of bees; when struck, it bestows death.
Resembling the flower of the linseed plant, pure and possessing the luster of the sky,
it causes hatred during great passion, and bestows the state of the wounded in purification, O beloved.

Resembling an indragopaka insect and possessing the luster of natural cinnabar, it is the performer of subjugation and attraction; indeed, the "woman's foot" (strīpada) is located in the station of the command (ājñā).
It possesses the luster of the rainbow of the Lord of Gods, is filled with a multitude of variegated colors,
and flows in a stream of prose and verse for the sake of Kṣepadeśvara.
Resembling the brilliant luster of a swan and equal in appearance to a topaz,
the syllable *huṃ* is situated on the path there at Sadāśiva, like the Ganges.
Extending upwards from Sadāśiva and situated below the All-pervading One (Vyāpaka),
it is the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the state of *pha* which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Pervasive, stainless, pure, and devoid of coming and going—by knowing which liberation occurs; that is called the half-measure (ardhamātrā). || 10 ||
Thus, the ninefold Vidyā is established within the nine wheels;
for him who knows it as residing within the body, accomplishment is not far off.
He who knows this shall undoubtedly know the sovereign of yoga;
it is divine, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation—one should not resort to any other state of being.
[Thus ends the Sūtra on the Visualization and Arrangement of the Nine-and-a-Half Syllables.]
